en: Majjhima Nikāya 150,
the Nagaravindeyya Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion, while the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he arrived at a village of the Kosalans named Nagaravinda.
The brahmin householders of Nagaravinda heard:

"Friends, the ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus and has arrived at Nagaravinda."
Furthermore, this excellent report of Master Gotama has spread abroad:

"Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
It is indeed good to see such Arahants.
Then the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Some, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One;
having concluded the courteous and amiable conversation, they sat down to one side.
Some extended their joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some [sat down] in the presence of the Blessed One.
Having announced their names and clans, they sat down to one side. Some sat down to one side in silence.
As the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda were sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to them:
"Householders, if wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:..."
‘Householders, what kind of ascetics and brahmins are not to be honored, respected, revered, or venerated?
Being asked this, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus:
‘Those ascetics and brahmins who are not free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye; internally—’
Those whose minds are unpeaceful act in an uneven manner through body, speech, and mind;
such ascetics and brahmins should not be honored, should not be revered, should not be respected, and should not be worshipped.
For what reason?

For we too are not free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye; our minds are unpacified within, and we conduct ourselves unevenly with body, speech, and mind. Even this even conduct of ours is seen as nothing more than that, for we perceive nothing superior to it.
Therefore, those venerable recluses and brahmins are not to be honored, not to be revered, not to be esteemed, and not to be worshipped.
As for those recluses and brahmins who [behave similarly] regarding sounds cognizable by the ear...
In odors cognizable by the nose...
in tastes cognizable by the tongue...
in tangibles cognizable by the body...
Those ascetics and brahmins who are not free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding mental phenomena; whose minds are inwardly unpacified;

and who conduct themselves with equanimity or inequality through body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins are not to be honored, not to be revered, not to be respected, and not to be worshipped.

And why is that? Because we ourselves are not yet free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding those things cognizable by the mind; our minds are not inwardly stilled, and we conduct ourselves with equanimity or lack thereof in body, speech, and mind. Thus, even our own practice of equanimity is something we do not see as superior to theirs.
Therefore, those venerable recluses and brahmins are not to be honored, revered, esteemed, or worshipped.’”
Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way.
But if, householders, wanderers of other sects were to ask you:
“In what manner, householders, are ascetics and brahmins worthy of being honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated? [you should answer:]
Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
"Those ascetics and brahmins who are free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye;
whose minds are internally stilled, and who practice even conduct with body, speech, and mind—such ascetics and brahmins [are those we honor]."
They are to be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.

And why is that? For we ourselves are not yet free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding forms cognizable by the eye; our minds are not inwardly stilled, and we conduct ourselves with equanimity or lack thereof through body, speech, and mind. Therefore, even this practice of ours toward those who see further is [worthy of respect].
Therefore, those venerable recluses and brahmins should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.
Those recluses and brahmins who [are skilled] regarding sounds cognizable by the ear...
regarding odors cognizable by the nose... [and so forth].
...toward tastes cognizable by the tongue ...
toward tangibles cognizable by the body ...
toward mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, they are free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion; with their minds inwardly stilled, they practice even conduct.
“Those ascetics and brahmins who act with body, speech, and mind in such a way—such persons should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped.

Why is that? Because we ourselves are not yet free from lust, not free from hatred, and not free from delusion regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind; our minds are not inwardly stilled, and we act with body, speech, and mind both rightly and wrongly. Therefore, even this practice of ours in accordance with what is right is something to be seen as superior.”
"Therefore, those venerable recluses and brahmins should be honored, revered, esteemed, and venerated.
If you householders are asked this by wanderers of other sects, you should answer them thus.
However, householders, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you this:
“What are the reasons, what are the grounds, venerable sirs, by which you say this:

‘Surely those venerable ones are either free from lust, or are practicing for the removal of lust; they are either free from hatred, or are practicing for the removal of hatred; they are either free from delusion, or are practicing for the removal of delusion’?
Being asked thus, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
"For these venerable ones resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats.
Yet there are no such forms cognizable by the eye there that they might take delight in upon seeing them again and again;
nor are there any such sounds cognizable by the ear there that they might take delight in upon hearing them again and again."
Moreover, there are no such odors cognizable by the nose there, which they might enjoy by smelling again and again;
nor are there any such flavors cognizable by the tongue there, which they might enjoy by tasting again and again;
nor are there any such tangibles cognizable by the body there, which they might enjoy by touching again and again.
“Friends, these are our reasons, these are our grounds, by which we say:

‘Surely those venerable ones are either free from lust, or are practicing for the removal of lust; they are either free from hatred, or are practicing for the removal of hatred; they are either free from delusion, or are practicing for the removal of delusion.
When questioned in this way, householders, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus.”
When this was said, the brahmin householders of Nagaravinda said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost...”
Or one who might show the way, or might hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways.
We go for refuge to Master Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“May the venerable Gotama accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The *Nagaravindeyya Sutta*, the eighth, is finished.
